quote_item6: Respondents from the DNR survey answered the following question: "Have you seen false or misleading information about any of the following topics, in the last week?"
quote_item10: Our final sample consists of 91,061 respondents from the DNR dataset that is matched and combined with respective country-level data from the V-DEM and GPS datasets.
notes: Reuters DNR 2021, 46 countries, samples representative of online populations - item 10 LOW (denominator is the real surveyed audience). Item 6 HIGH: the construct is explicitly perceived exposure, 'information that lacks facticity in the eyes of the individual, regardless of its actual facticity' - no external ground truth at all, so this is not a source-level-list case and the new ruling does not apply. Item 7 HIGH: single unvalidated self-report item, never benchmarked against actual exposure. Item 3 HIGH: YouGov opt-in online panels with quotas, not probability sampling. Item 4 HIGH: no response or attrition rates reported and panel self-selection not addressed.

notes: Abstract only (no cached full text). Item 6 LOW: accuracy judged against current clinical knowledge/ACOG guidance by a clinician reviewer with second-reviewer consensus = expert-verified false claims, which item 6 lists as acceptable; this is direct incorrectness, not a DISCERN/GQS-style quality instrument. Lowest-confidence call in this shard - the abstract itself does not name the external standard. Items 1-3 HIGH: top-100-by-search-algorithm videos under three hashtags is a curated, popularity-ranked topical corpus. Item 7 HIGH: no reliability statistic reported. Item 9 HIGH: no collection window stated in the abstract; single search snapshot. Item 10 HIGH: 298 curated videos, no audience or view weighting, presented as the misinformation share.

quote_item6: Focusing on content characteristics, we examined the range of topics, valence, and facticity of the messages forwarded to the WhatsApp group to be fact-checked.
quote_item10: This study is based on a content analysis of 238 forwarded messages sent to a public fact-checking group on WhatsApp in Singapore during the first six months of the COVID-19 pandemic
notes: Abstract only (no cached full text). Items 1-2 HIGH: the universe is messages users chose to submit to a fact-checking service - selection on suspected falsity, i.e. on the outcome. Item 10 HIGH for the same reason: '49% inaccurate' is a share of a self-selected suspicious-message pool, in no sense an audience denominator. Item 6 LOW: facticity rests on fact-checker verdicts of the submitted messages (external ground truth); low confidence from the abstract alone as to whether the researchers or the fact-checkers assigned the verdicts. Item 7 HIGH: no reliability statistic visible. Item 3 LOW: complete census of the 238 submissions. Item 9 LOW: six-month window stated.

quote_item6: Factual videos were defined as those discussing information validated through a literature review and consultation with an expert in rhinology (C.R.R.), while nonfactual videos discussed nonvalidated information.
quote_item10: From 465 initial videos, 220 videos were included in this study.
notes: Item 6 HIGH: the standard is a literature review run by the authors plus a single in-house co-author expert - internal and ad hoc, not an external pre-existing standard; and 'nonfactual' is defined as NONVALIDATED rather than false, i.e. absence of evidence standing in for falsity. The paper is framed as a quality review and also applies PEMAT/GQS. Item 7 HIGH: two reviewers with a third resolving disagreements but no kappa/alpha reported and no validated factuality instrument. Items 1-3 HIGH: first 155 algorithm-recommended videos per hashtag, i.e. popularity-ranked curated topical corpus. Item 9 HIGH: single-day capture (searched TikTok 29-30 January 2023) generalised to prevalence. Item 10 HIGH: 220 curated videos, no view weighting.
